events.text: The rain comes down on the market like thrown rice. You are standing under a butcher's awning with forty other people when {npc} steps out of a bookshop, looks at you, and holds out an oil-paper umbrella painted with plum blossom. 'Bring it back when it stops,' {he} says, and runs off into the rain without one.

choices.text: Take it, and learn where the bookshop keeper lives

mem.note: took my umbrella and my word

effects.log: The umbrella keeps you dry all the way home. It smells faintly of ink and pine resin. You stand it by the door like a guest.

choices.text: Run after {npc} and hold it over you both

mem.note: ran after me in the rain

effects.log: You catch {npc} at the bridge. The umbrella is not big enough for two. Neither of you mentions it.

choices.text: Refuse politely. A stranger should keep their umbrella

effects.log: {npc} shrugs, opens the umbrella, and walks away dry. You stand under the awning for another hour, thinking.

events.text: You meant to return the umbrella the next day. It has been a month. Every time you go to the bookshop, you lose your nerve at the door and buy a book instead. You now own eleven books on irrigation. {npc} has noticed.

choices.text: Walk in and return it, with a pear

mem.note: brought back the umbrella with a pear

effects.log: {npc} takes the umbrella, then the pear, then laughs. 'Eleven books on irrigation. I thought you were planning a canal.'

choices.text: Leave it at the door with a note

mem.note: left me a note I kept

ok.log: The note is three lines long and took you all night. The next morning there is an answer pinned to your own door.

fail.log: A dog takes the note. The umbrella stays. {npc} thinks you are a thief, or very strange, and is not sure which is worse.

choices.text: Keep it. Some things are not returned

effects.log: The umbrella stays by your door. {npc} stops looking up when you pass the shop. You keep buying books anyway.

events.text: It rains again, the same thrown-rice rain. You are under the butcher's awning, and so is {npc}, without an umbrella, holding a parcel of books against the wet. You have the plum-blossom umbrella in your hand. You always carry it now.

choices.text: Hold it out. Bring it back when it stops

mem.note: gave me back my own umbrella

effects.log: {npc} looks at the umbrella, then at you, and does not take it. 'Walk me home,' {he} says. It does not stop raining for a long time.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to marry you, under the awning, in front of everyone

mem.note: asked me under the butcher's awning

effects.log: The butcher drops a cleaver. Forty wet people hold their breath. {npc} says yes, and the whole awning cheers.

choices.text: Give it back for good, and walk away in the rain

effects.log: You get very wet. {npc} keeps the umbrella this time. Some stories are only about an umbrella, and that is fine.

events.text: Under a loose stone of the old bridge you find a letter, folded small, addressed to nobody. It is a poem about the moon, and it is terrible, and somebody worked very hard on it. In the corner: 'If anyone reads this, write back.'

choices.text: Write back, with a terrible poem of your own

effects.log: Your poem is about a duck. You leave it under the stone and feel foolish for three days. On the fourth, there is an answer.

choices.text: Write back, and correct the rhymes

effects.log: You fix the rhymes in red ink. The next letter is furious, and then, at the bottom, grateful, and asks about the second verse.

choices.text: Put the stone back and leave it be

effects.log: You leave the letter where it was. Someone, somewhere, waits for an answer that does not come. You feel it on your way home.

events.text: Forty letters now, under the stone, in a year. You know the writer hates winter, loves dumplings with chives, and once cried at a puppet show. You do not know a name. The last letter says: 'Tomorrow at dawn. I will be the one with the bad poem.'

choices.text: Go at dawn

effects.log: On the bridge stands {npc}, holding a sheet of paper upside down, shaking. You recognise the handwriting before the face.

choices.text: Go early and hide under the bridge to look first

ok.log: You see {npc} arrive, pace, practise a bow, trip on the practice. You come up from under the bridge laughing, and {he} does too.

fail.log: You slip into the river. {npc} fishes you out with a broom. The first meeting is very wet and very memorable.

choices.text: Do not go. The letters are enough

effects.log: You stay home. The next letter under the stone says only: 'I understand.' It is the last one.

events.text: You and {npc} still leave letters under the bridge stone, though you see each other every day now. The stone has been worn smooth by your hands. Today the letter under it is not a poem. It is one line: 'Ask me.'

choices.text: Ask

effects.log: You ask on the bridge, out loud, badly. {npc} says yes in writing, under the stone, the next morning, so it is official.

choices.text: Write your answer under the stone instead

mem.note: wrote me a reply I keep

effects.log: Your letter is the best thing you have ever written. {npc} reads it on the bridge and keeps it in a sleeve for the rest of {his} life.

choices.text: Say you are not ready

effects.log: {npc} nods and says nothing. The letters keep coming, but shorter, as if the paper were dearer.

events.text: You have been bringing persimmons to {npc} for a month. Today there is already a basket of persimmons on the step, bigger than yours, with a red ribbon. Across the street a young sword student named Gong is pretending to read a notice board.

choices.text: Leave your basket beside Gong's, bigger or not

effects.log: Two baskets on the step. {npc} comes out, looks at them, looks at you both, and takes one persimmon from each.

choices.text: Challenge Gong to a persimmon-carrying race

ok.log: You win by a nose, with the whole street cheering. {npc} watches from the window, trying very hard not to laugh.

fail.log: Gong wins. You drop forty persimmons in the street. Children eat them. {npc} sends you a cloth for your scraped knees.

choices.text: Leave. Two baskets is a quarrel waiting

effects.log: You take your persimmons home and eat them all. They are very good. You are not sure you did the right thing.

events.text: Gong turns up at your door at midnight with a jar of wine. 'It is no use,' Gong says. '{npc} talks about you. All the time. Even when I bring persimmons.' Gong sits on your step and sighs like a bellows.

choices.text: Make tea and hear Gong out

effects.log: By dawn you are friends. Gong gives you the name of the best persimmon tree in the province, which is a great sacrifice.

choices.text: Tell Gong not to give up

effects.log: Gong goes away comforted, and brings bigger baskets. You start to regret your honesty around the fourth one.

choices.text: Thank Gong and close the door

effects.log: Gong sighs on the step until sunrise and then goes home. The street thinks you have a ghost.

events.text: {npc} asks to see you at the willow by the canal. When you arrive, Gong is there too, hat in hand. {npc} looks at the two of you for a long moment and says, 'One of you is going to have to say something useful.'

choices.text: Say what you feel, plainly, in front of Gong

effects.log: You say it. Gong puts on a hat and says, 'Well. That was useful.' Gong leaves. {npc} does not.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to marry you, and Gong to stand witness

mem.note: asked me with Gong as witness

effects.log: Gong stands witness at the wedding and weeps more than anyone, and brings persimmons. Of course.

choices.text: Say Gong has the better heart

mem.note: gave me away like a basket

effects.log: {npc} narrows {his} eyes. 'I decide whose heart is better,' {he} says, and walks off, and you have made two people angry at once.

events.text: {npc}, who runs the noodle stall by the east gate, has said in your hearing that {he} could never love anyone who cannot cook. You have never cooked anything. You once burned water. You buy a pot.

choices.text: Practise in secret every night

effects.log: Your neighbours smell smoke for a month. One of them leaves a bucket of water at your door, as a hint.

choices.text: Ask {npc} for cooking lessons, honestly

effects.log: {npc} laughs so hard the noodles boil over. Then: 'Tomorrow. Before dawn. Bring your own knife.'

choices.text: Hire a cook and pass it off as yours (20 taels)

effects.log: The dumplings are perfect. Too perfect. {npc} eats one and looks at you very thoughtfully. (-20 taels)

events.text: Today you cook for {npc}. The kitchen is full of smoke and possibility. The rice is going wrong in a way you do not have a word for.

choices.text: Serve it anyway, with a straight face

mem.note: served me burnt rice like a banquet

ok.log: {npc} eats the whole bowl. 'Terrible,' {he} says. 'Make it again next week.'

fail.log: {npc} takes one bite and has to sit down. Then {he} gets up, and cooks for you instead, scolding the whole time.

choices.text: Throw it out and make plain porridge

effects.log: Plain porridge, with a little ginger. {npc} says it is honest food, which from {him} is high praise.

choices.text: Confess about the hired cook

mem.note: told me the truth about the dumplings

effects.log: {npc} already knew. 'The dumplings had a fold you cannot do,' {he} says. 'Nobody can, but old Liu.' Then {he} laughs.

events.text: A year of lessons, and you can make noodles that do not fall apart. Today you stand at the stall while {npc} is ill, and the whole east gate queues for your noodles. Some of them even come back for more.

choices.text: Take the noodles to {npc}, and ask the question

mem.note: kept my stall and asked me

effects.log: {npc} eats the noodles in bed, says they are too salty, and says yes. The stall's sign has two names on it by spring.

choices.text: Keep the stall going until {npc} is well

effects.log: Ten days at the stall. When {npc} comes back, the till is full and the regulars ask after you. {npc} looks at you differently now.

choices.text: Close the stall and nurse {npc}

mem.note: shut the stall to sit with me

effects.log: You make porridge. It is very good porridge. {npc} says nothing, but the next day takes your hand and does not let go.

events.text: On the bamboo bridge outside town a stranger blocks your way: {npc}, sword on the shoulder, grinning. 'Only one of us crosses first,' {he} says. It is a very narrow bridge. It is also a very silly reason to fight.

choices.text: Cross swords, for the fun of it

ok.log: You win, barely. {npc} laughs from the stream below. 'Same time next year,' {he} calls.

mem.note: lost to me on the bridge

fail.log: You end up in the stream. {npc} crosses, then comes back and offers a hand. 'Same time next year.'

choices.text: Bow and let {npc} go first

effects.log: {npc} looks almost disappointed, crosses, and turns at the far end. 'Next year you fight me,' {he} says.

choices.text: Find a ford downstream

effects.log: You wade the ford and get on with your day. You hear {npc} laughing on the bridge for a long while.

events.text: A year on, the same bridge. {npc} is already there, with two cups and a flask of wine on the rail. 'I trained all year for this,' {he} says. So did you. The leaves are falling like they did last time.

choices.text: Fight properly, all out

ok.log: A long fight, and a draw. You both end up sitting on the bridge, breathless, drinking water from the river.

fail.log: {npc} wins clean. Then pours you a cup of tea, and tells you exactly what you did wrong, kindly, for an hour.

choices.text: Talk first. Fight after

effects.log: You never get to the fight. You talk until the moon rises. The swords lie on the rail like two cats asleep.

choices.text: Bring your own tea, better than {his} wine

effects.log: Your tea is better. {npc} admits it, grudgingly, and then drinks most of it. (-5 taels)

events.text: The fifth year of the bridge. {npc} arrives without a sword. 'I am tired of fighting you,' {he} says, and looks at the water. 'I would rather walk beside you for a while. Across. And then further.'

choices.text: Walk with {npc}, across and further

mem.note: walked across the bridge with me for good

effects.log: You are married by the winter. At the wedding the two swords hang crossed over the door, which the guests find either romantic or alarming.

choices.text: Take {npc}'s hand, but keep your sword

mem.note: took my hand and kept the sword

effects.log: 'Good,' {npc} says. 'I would think less of you otherwise.' You walk across together, armed and happy.

choices.text: Say you came to fight

effects.log: {npc} sighs, borrows a stick, and beats you with it. Then goes home. Next year {he} does not come.

events.text: Lantern Festival. On the riddle lanterns of the Wang family's gate, one riddle has hung unanswered for three years. You reach for the slip at the same moment as {npc}. Your fingers touch. Neither of you lets go.

choices.text: Answer it together, whispering

ok.log: The answer is 'a shadow'. Old Wang gives you a lantern shaped like a rabbit and makes you share it.

fail.log: You are both wrong, loudly and differently. Old Wang laughs and gives you each a bean cake for trying.

choices.text: Let go and let {npc} take it

effects.log: {npc} reads it, frowns, and then hands it back to you. 'Help me,' {he} says. That is how it starts.

choices.text: Snatch it and run

effects.log: You run off with the riddle and solve it alone at home. You win a rabbit lantern and nobody to show it to.

events.text: Every Lantern Festival since, you and {npc} meet at the Wang gate. This year {npc} has written a riddle of {his} own and hung it among the others. It is meant for you, and it is very hard.

choices.text: Stay up all night to solve it

effects.log: By dawn you have it. The answer is your own name, written as a riddle. You go to find {npc} with your hair standing up.

choices.text: Ask the old men at the teahouse

effects.log: The old men solve it in a breath and laugh at you for an hour. The answer is your own name.

choices.text: Write a riddle back, harder

effects.log: {npc} spends a month on it and comes to your door, furious, with the answer: {his} own name. You both laugh in the street.

events.text: The rabbit lantern from the first year still hangs at your door, faded pink. At the Wang gate tonight there is one new riddle slip, in your handwriting, and {npc} is reading it with both hands.

choices.text: The answer is a question. Wait for {his} reply

effects.log: {npc} reads it twice and turns, and says the answer out loud, which is yes. Old Wang lights every lantern on the gate.

choices.text: Take the slip back. Say it plainly instead

effects.log: 'You could have just said that years ago,' {npc} says, and holds the rabbit lantern so you both fit in its light.

choices.text: Let it hang unanswered another year

effects.log: {npc} reads it and does not answer. Maybe next year. The lanterns go out one by one.

events.text: You limp into the clinic with a sword cut on your arm. The physician, {npc}, looks at it, looks at you, and says, 'Who taught you to block like that? A goose?' Then {he} stitches it so gently you hardly feel it.

choices.text: Defend your blocking

effects.log: {npc} lets you argue, ties the last knot and says, 'A goose. I stand by it.' You leave smiling for no reason.

choices.text: Ask {npc} how to block properly

effects.log: {npc} shows you, with a broom, in the clinic doorway. It is better advice than your last teacher's.

choices.text: Pay and leave quietly (5 taels)

effects.log: The arm heals clean. You think about the voice for a week, and then do not. (-5 taels)

events.text: You are back at the clinic for the fourth time this season. A twisted ankle, a bruise, a splinter you could have pulled yourself. {npc} folds {his} arms. 'Either you are the clumsiest fighter in the province, or you are here on purpose.'

choices.text: Admit it is on purpose

effects.log: {npc} goes red to the ears and throws a roll of bandage at you. Then says the clinic closes at sundown, if you were wondering.

choices.text: Insist you are just clumsy

ok.log: {npc} does not believe a word, and says so, and tells you to come back tomorrow for a check you do not need.

fail.log: {npc} believes you, sadly, and gives you a long lecture on footwork and a bitter tea. You drink it all.

choices.text: Bring flowers instead of an injury

effects.log: {npc} puts the flowers in a medicine jar and says it is a waste of a good jar, and keeps them a month.

events.text: You come home from a real fight with a real wound. {npc} meets you at the clinic door, white as rice paper, and for once does not scold you at all. {He} stitches in silence. At the last knot {his} hands are shaking.

choices.text: Take {his} hands and ask {npc} to marry you

mem.note: asked me with my own stitches in

effects.log: 'Only if you promise to block better,' {npc} says, crying and laughing. You promise. You mostly keep it.

choices.text: Promise to come home whole

effects.log: {npc} holds you to it. From then on there is always a bag of bandages in your pack, in {his} handwriting.

choices.text: Joke about the goose

effects.log: {npc} laughs once, a wet laugh, and slaps your good arm. Not yet, then. But soon.

events.text: The ferry over the Grey River is poled by {npc}, who has a voice like a temple bell and sings the whole way across. Everyone pays one copper. You find yourself crossing the river four times a day for no reason at all.

choices.text: Sing along

mem.note: sang with me on the ferry

ok.log: Your voice is not a temple bell. It is more of a pot lid. {npc} laughs so hard the ferry turns in a circle.

fail.log: You sing badly enough that a goose answers. {npc} sings louder, to cover you, and winks.

choices.text: Offer to take a turn at the pole

effects.log: You pole the ferry into a sandbank. {npc} gets it off with one push and does not let you forget it.

choices.text: Cross once and go about your business

effects.log: You cross the river once, like a sensible person. The singing follows you up the bank.

events.text: Spring flood. The river is brown and fast, and the magistrate has forbidden the ferry. {npc} sits on the bank beside the tied boat, not singing. Without the ferry there is no money, and without money there is no rice.

choices.text: Bring rice, without making a speech about it

effects.log: You leave a sack by the boat. {npc} pretends not to know who left it, and sings that night, quietly. (-8 taels)

choices.text: Help mend the ferry while it waits

effects.log: A week of tar and rope. The ferry has never been so sound. Neither, says {npc}, has the ferryman's mood.

choices.text: Sit on the bank too

effects.log: You sit together and watch the flood. Neither of you says much. By evening {npc} is humming.

events.text: The river is calm. On the ferry today {npc} stops in the middle, where the water is deepest and slowest, and lays the pole across the boat. 'Everybody pays one copper,' {he} says. 'You have paid about three thousand. I owe you a crossing.'

choices.text: Ask for a crossing that lasts

mem.note: asked me in the middle of the river

effects.log: You are married on the ferry, which drifts the whole time. The guests have to wade to the feast. Nobody minds.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to sing the song from the first day

effects.log: {npc} sings it, slowly, to you and nobody else, and the ferry drifts a long way downstream before anyone notices.

choices.text: Pay one copper, as always

effects.log: {npc} takes the copper and picks up the pole. 'One day,' {he} says, and sings the rest of the way.

events.text: On the wall of a mountain pavilion someone has written half a poem in a fine hand: two lines about a crane that will not land. Under it, in the same hand: 'For whoever can finish it.' {npc} is sitting in the pavilion, pretending to read.

choices.text: Write the next two lines on the wall

ok.log: Your crane lands, at last, on a cold river. {npc} reads it over your shoulder and goes very quiet.

fail.log: Your lines rhyme 'crane' with 'rain' and then with 'again'. {npc} groans aloud, then laughs, then corrects you on the wall.

choices.text: Ask {npc} who wrote it

effects.log: 'Nobody important,' {npc} says, and blushes. It was {npc}. You decide to come back tomorrow.

choices.text: Leave the poem unfinished

effects.log: Some cranes do not land. You walk on down the mountain with the two lines in your head for a week.

events.text: You and {npc} have been finishing each other's poems on the pavilion wall all year. Travellers come up the mountain to read them. Somebody has copied the wall into a book and is selling it in town, with both your names spelled wrong.

choices.text: Go to town and demand a share

effects.log: The bookseller pays you to go away, and then pays you to sign the next printing. {npc} laughs at the spelling. (+15 taels)

choices.text: Let the book go. Write a new wall

effects.log: You start a new wall, on the far side, where only the two of you know to look.

choices.text: Write one poem only for {npc}, not for the wall

mem.note: wrote me a poem nobody else read

effects.log: It is the first poem you have written that is not clever. {npc} folds it into a sleeve and does not show anyone.

events.text: The pavilion wall is full. There is one space left, low down, near the floor. {npc} has written two lines there: a crane that has found somewhere to land, and the place is not a river. The last two lines are yours to write.

choices.text: Write a proposal in two lines

mem.note: finished the wall with a proposal

effects.log: {npc} reads them, takes the brush, and writes one word under them, very large. Travellers still come to read it.

choices.text: Write that you will land there too

effects.log: Two cranes on one line of poem. {npc} takes your arm on the way down the mountain and keeps it.

choices.text: Leave the space empty

effects.log: You cannot find the words. {npc} waits a long while, then washes the brush and goes home alone.

events.text: {npc} has decided the courtyard needs a garden. You agree. You do not agree on anything else: {npc} wants peonies. You want cabbages. The courtyard is exactly big enough for one argument.

choices.text: Peonies. Beauty first

effects.log: The peonies come up like a festival. The neighbours stop to look. You eat bought cabbage and do not complain, much.

choices.text: Cabbages. A house must eat

effects.log: The cabbages are magnificent and {npc} is not speaking to them. (+5 taels saved on vegetables)

choices.text: Half and half, with a line of stones

effects.log: A border of white stones. Peonies on one side, cabbages on the other, glaring at each other like rival sects.

events.text: A caterpillar plague. Something is eating the garden by night, both halves, peony and cabbage alike. {npc} has been sitting up with a lantern. So, it turns out, have you, on the other side of the wall.

choices.text: Sit up together

effects.log: You catch caterpillars by lantern light until dawn, two grown martial artists in their nightclothes, laughing.

choices.text: Ask an old farmer for a cure

effects.log: Ash and garlic water, says the farmer. It works. The garden smells like a cookhouse for a month.

choices.text: Let the caterpillars have the peonies

effects.log: The cabbages survive. The peonies do not. {npc} is very polite to you for a week, which is worse.

events.text: Years on, the stone border between peonies and cabbages is gone. Somewhere along the way the two halves grew into each other. A visitor asks who planned such a strange, lovely garden. You and {npc} look at each other.

choices.text: Say {npc} planned it

mem.note: gave me the credit for the garden

effects.log: {npc} says you are a liar and squeezes your hand under the table.

choices.text: Say the caterpillars did

mem.note: made me laugh in front of a guest

effects.log: The visitor does not understand. You and {npc} laugh until the tea goes cold.

choices.text: Plant one thing together, for the next years

mem.note: planted a plum tree with me

effects.log: A plum sapling, by the gate. It will take ten years to fruit. You both mean to be there.

events.text: {npc} says you snore. You say you do not. {npc} says you snore like a water buffalo in a cave. You say {he} would know, since {he} snores like two. Neither of you has slept properly in a week.

choices.text: Sleep in the study, to prove a point

effects.log: The study is cold and the chair is a liar. In the morning {npc} says it was too quiet to sleep.

choices.text: Ask a servant to listen and judge

effects.log: The servant listens all night and reports, red-faced, that you both snore, in turns, like a duet.

choices.text: Buy a herbal pillow said to cure snoring (6 taels)

effects.log: The pillow smells of chrysanthemum and cures nothing. You both sleep beautifully on it anyway. (-6 taels)

events.text: A guest stays the night: an old sworn friend of {npc}'s, a famous swordsman. At breakfast the swordsman, very tired, asks if the house is haunted, because something was roaring in the night like a tiger with a cold.

choices.text: Blame {npc}, in front of the guest

effects.log: {npc} blames you. The swordsman blames both. It is the most cheerful breakfast the house has ever had.

choices.text: Say it was the house tiger, and keep a straight face

ok.log: The swordsman believes you and tells the whole murim your house keeps a tiger. Your fame grows, strangely.

fail.log: Nobody believes you. {npc} chokes on {his} rice. The swordsman leaves early, and laughing.

choices.text: Confess you both do

effects.log: The swordsman confesses too. It turns out everyone snores, and nobody has ever told anyone.

events.text: You are away a month on business. On the first night you cannot sleep at all. The inn is too quiet. On the second night you realise what is missing, and you are a little embarrassed.

choices.text: Write to {npc} and admit it

mem.note: wrote that the inn was too quiet

effects.log: {npc} writes back: 'Me too. I have been sleeping with the window open to hear the ox next door.'

choices.text: Hurry home early

effects.log: You come home three days early. That night the house roars like two tigers, and you sleep like a stone.

choices.text: Hire the inn's noisiest guest to share your room

effects.log: A cloth merchant who snores like a landslide. You sleep wonderfully. You tell {npc} about it later and are scolded.

events.text: You come home whistling. The table is laid with eight dishes, two candles and the good wine. {npc} is sitting at it, very still. You have no idea what day it is. You have a very strong feeling that you should.

choices.text: Pretend you knew all along

ok.log: You get away with it, through a speech that makes no sense. {npc} knows. {He} lets you have it, this once.

mem.note: forgot our day and lied about it

fail.log: You guess the wrong festival. Very wrong. The good wine goes back in the cupboard, unopened.

choices.text: Admit you forgot, and ask what day it is

mem.note: forgot our day but owned it

effects.log: It is the day you met. {npc} tells you about it, all of it, over eight cold dishes. You remember it now.

choices.text: Run out and come back with a gift (15 taels)

effects.log: A jade comb, bought at a run. {npc} says it is lovely and that you have rice on your sleeve. (-15 taels)

events.text: The day comes round again. This time you have marked it on the doorpost, on your sleeve and on the inside of your sword sheath. You will not forget. The only question is how to do better than eight dishes.

choices.text: Cook the eight dishes yourself

effects.log: Six of the dishes are edible. {npc} eats all eight, and says the burnt one is the best, and means it.

choices.text: Take {npc} back to where you met

mem.note: took me back to where we met

effects.log: The place has changed. A noodle shop where the old wall was. You eat noodles there, and it is perfect.

choices.text: Write down every year since, one line each

effects.log: It takes all night. Some years are only one word. {npc} reads it twice, and adds the lines you forgot.

events.text: Many years married. {npc} comes home with a strange smile, leads you to the table, and there are eight dishes, two candles and the good wine. 'Do you know what day it is?' {he} asks. You do. You have known every year since.

choices.text: Say the day, and the year, and the weather

effects.log: {npc} laughs and cries a little, and the two of you are old and foolish at the table till midnight.

choices.text: Pretend to forget, for the joke

effects.log: {npc} sees through it in a breath and throws a dumpling at you. The good wine is opened anyway.

events.text: {npc} wants to learn the sword. From you. Every martial artist knows you never teach your own spouse: it ends in tears, or a wound, or both. {npc} is already standing in the courtyard with a broom handle.

choices.text: Teach {npc}, properly, as a master

effects.log: The first lesson ends in a quarrel about stance. The second in laughter. The third in a bruise. {npc} comes back for the fourth.

choices.text: Teach {npc}, gently, as a spouse

effects.log: {npc} notices at once that you are going easy. 'I did not marry you for gentle,' {he} says, and hits you with the broom.

choices.text: Find {npc} another teacher (20 taels)

effects.log: The teacher is very good and {npc} is very annoyed with you about it, for some reason. (-20 taels)

events.text: A year of lessons. This morning {npc} asks for a real spar, no holding back. There is a look in {his} eyes you have seen in good opponents, just before they surprise you.

choices.text: Spar, all out

ok.log: You win, but only just, and only because {npc} stops to laugh at a clever feint of {his} own. It was clever.

fail.log: {npc} catches you on the wrist and you drop your sword in the koi pond. {He} is insufferable for a week.

choices.text: Let {npc} win, subtly

effects.log: {npc} knows instantly. {He} puts the broom away and does not ask to spar again for a month.

choices.text: Teach a trick you never showed anyone

effects.log: Your own secret turn of the wrist. {npc} learns it in a morning. You feel proud and slightly robbed.

events.text: Bandits on the road home, four of them, at dusk. Before you can draw, {npc} has stepped in front of you with a borrowed staff and the stance you taught. The bandits look at the two of you, side by side, and reconsider their evening.

choices.text: Fight back to back

mem.note: fought back to back with me

ok.log: It is over very quickly. On the walk home {npc} cannot stop talking about it, and neither can you.

mem.note: fought back to back with me

fail.log: You both take a bruise or two, and the bandits run. {npc} binds your arm with {his} sash, grinning.

choices.text: Let {npc} handle it

effects.log: {npc} handles it. Two bandits in the ditch, two running. You applaud. {npc} bows like a sect master.

choices.text: Pay the bandits off and go home (10 taels)

mem.note: paid them off when I was ready

effects.log: The bandits take the silver and go. {npc} is very disappointed in you. (-10 taels)

events.text: A fever goes through the town in the twelfth month, and {npc} takes it badly. The physician says rest, warmth and time, and that the next three nights will tell. {npc} is cross about being in bed, which you choose to take as a good sign.

choices.text: Sit up with {npc}, every night

mem.note: sat up with me in the fever

effects.log: Three nights of cool cloths and bad jokes. On the third dawn the fever breaks, and {npc} asks for noodles.

choices.text: Ride for the best physician in the province (30 taels)

mem.note: rode for a physician for me

effects.log: The famous physician arrives, looks at {npc} and says the local physician was right. You pay anyway, happily. (-30 taels)

choices.text: Brew a medicine yourself from an old recipe

ok.log: The medicine tastes like a burned shoe and works overnight. {npc} says {he} will never forgive the taste.

fail.log: The medicine does nothing but make {npc} laugh at the smell. The fever breaks on its own. The laughing may have helped.

events.text: {npc} is well again, and has been strangely quiet. Tonight {he} says it: in the fever, {he} dreamed of your house without {him} in it, and you alone at the table. {He} wants to know what you would do.

choices.text: Answer honestly

effects.log: You say you would keep the house as it is and set two cups every night. {npc} takes your hand and does not let go.

choices.text: Say you would follow {him} the next day

effects.log: {npc} says that is the most foolish thing you have ever said and forbids it. Then hugs you for a long time.

choices.text: Say you will not let it come to that

effects.log: Next morning you are out buying the warmest quilt in the market. {npc} is under it by evening, pretending to be annoyed.

events.text: Winter again. The same fever comes back to town. This time it is you lying in bed, and {npc} at the bedside with a cool cloth, a bowl of noodles and a long list of every bad joke you told {him} last time.

choices.text: Laugh at every joke

mem.note: laughed at my jokes in the fever

effects.log: Laughing is a good medicine. The fever breaks on the second night. The jokes do not improve.

choices.text: Be a terrible patient

effects.log: You complain about everything. {npc} is delighted: {he} has waited years for this. You both recover.

events.text: Fixing a loose floorboard, you find a jar of silver hidden under it, a lot of silver, in small coins, saved over years. Nobody in the house has said a word about it. {npc} is out at the market.

choices.text: Put it back exactly as it was

effects.log: You put the board back and say nothing. You notice, after that, how often {npc} goes without things.

choices.text: Ask {npc} about it at supper

effects.log: {npc} goes red, then pale, and says it is for something, and that you will see, and will not say more.

choices.text: Count it, out of curiosity

effects.log: Three hundred and twelve coins, wrapped in a cloth embroidered with your name. You put it back very carefully.

events.text: The jar is gone from under the floor. That evening {npc} leads you to the gate. There is a horse there, a real one, a good bay with a white blaze, the kind you stopped yourself wanting years ago because you could not afford it.

choices.text: Ride it round the town, whooping

effects.log: The whole street sees you, and you do not care. {npc} watches from the gate, arms folded, very satisfied.

choices.text: Say {npc} should have spent it on {him}self

effects.log: 'This is on myself,' {npc} says. 'I wanted to see your face.' You stop arguing. The horse eats your hat.

choices.text: Start a jar of your own the next morning

effects.log: A jar under a different floorboard. You think {npc} has not seen it. {npc} has seen it.

events.text: Years later, mending another loose board, {npc} finds your jar. You have been saving for a long time. It holds enough for something {npc} once mentioned wanting, once, a long time ago, and never again.

choices.text: Give it now, though it is not yet the day

effects.log: A small house on the lake where {npc} grew up, for summers. {npc} cannot speak for a while. (-40 taels)

choices.text: Pretend the jar is not yours

mem.note: played the jar game with me

effects.log: {npc} puts the board back and says nothing, with the same face you wore years ago. The game goes on.

events.text: Two bamboo chairs on the veranda, side by side. Every evening you and {npc} sit there and watch the road. Tonight {npc} says the chairs are getting old, and that so are you, and asks if you want new chairs.

choices.text: Keep the old chairs

effects.log: The chairs creak in a familiar way. {npc} says they creak in your voice. You say they creak in {his}.

choices.text: Make new chairs with your own hands

effects.log: The new chairs are slightly lopsided. {npc} sits in one and declares it the best chair under heaven.

choices.text: Buy a single long bench instead (8 taels)

effects.log: A bench means you sit closer. {npc} notices and says nothing, and leans a little. (-8 taels)

events.text: On the veranda {npc} asks the question old people ask: what was the best year? Not the most famous. The best.

choices.text: Name a year from the very beginning

effects.log: You both remember it differently. You argue happily about who said what on which bridge until the stars come out.

choices.text: Say this one

mem.note: said this year was the best

effects.log: {npc} laughs and calls you a flatterer. But {he} stops arguing, and holds your hand on the arm of the chair.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to answer first

effects.log: {npc} names a year you had forgotten: a bad year, poor and cold, when you had only each other. You remember now.

events.text: A very old swordsman walks up the road and stops at your gate: someone you fought, long ago, when you were both young and fierce. The old swordsman looks at the two of you on the veranda for a while. 'So this is how it ended for you.'

choices.text: Invite him up for tea

effects.log: The old swordsman stays till dark and tells {npc} stories about you that you had hoped were forgotten. {npc} is delighted.

choices.text: Tell him it has not ended yet

effects.log: The old swordsman laughs, bows, and walks on. {npc} pours you another cup. 'Not yet,' {he} agrees.

events.text: A travelling painter offers to paint you and {npc} together, for the hall. It will take six sittings. You must both sit still for an hour each time, side by side, without speaking. You have never done that in your lives.

choices.text: Sit for it (25 taels)

effects.log: The first sitting lasts four breaths before {npc} makes you laugh. The painter sighs a painter's sigh. (-25 taels)

choices.text: Haggle the painter down (12 taels)

ok.log: Half price, if you promise to sit still. You promise. It is a lie. (-12 taels)

fail.log: The painter takes offence and leaves, and paints your neighbour instead, very flatteringly.

choices.text: Say you would rather keep your faces to yourselves

effects.log: The painter shrugs and leaves. {npc} draws you both on a scrap of paper that night. It is terrible. You keep it.

events.text: The portrait is finished. The painter unveils it in the hall. You are both perfectly painted, and both perfectly solemn, and neither of you looks like yourself at all. {npc} is staring at it in silent horror.

choices.text: Ask the painter to add one thing: a smile

mem.note: asked for a smile in the portrait

effects.log: The painter adds the smallest smile to each face. It is better. It is you now. (-5 taels)

choices.text: Hang it in the hall and laugh at it every day

mem.note: laughed at our portrait with me

effects.log: Guests bow respectfully to the stern portrait. You and {npc} hide behind the screen, laughing.

choices.text: Draw the two of you yourself, and hang it beside

mem.note: hung a true picture of us

effects.log: Two portraits, one fine and false, one badly drawn and true. Every guest asks about the second one.

events.text: Thirty years on, a neighbour's child stands in front of the old wedding portrait, and asks who those two stern strangers are. {npc}, much older now, looks at you sideways.

choices.text: Tell the true story of the six sittings

effects.log: The child laughs so hard that the whole house comes running. The portrait has never been so loved.

choices.text: Say they were very serious ancestors

effects.log: The child bows deeply to the portrait. {npc} has to leave the room. You are both very bad ancestors.

events.text: A grey stray cat walks into the house, inspects every room, and chooses {npc}. It will sit only on {his} lap, eat only from {his} bowl and stare at you with open contempt. {npc} is thrilled. You are, somehow, jealous of a cat.

choices.text: Win the cat over with dried fish

effects.log: The cat eats the fish, looks at you, and goes and sits on {npc}. You have been used. (-2 taels)

choices.text: Pretend not to care

ok.log: The cat is offended by your indifference and sits on you out of spite. {npc} is furious. Victory.

fail.log: The cat does not notice you not caring. It does not notice you at all. {npc} laughs at you every evening.

choices.text: Name the cat after your old rival

effects.log: The cat is now called Iron Fist Wang. It answers to it. {npc} cannot say the name without laughing.

events.text: {npc} has to travel for a month. The cat and you are left alone in the house, and you look at each other across the empty courtyard like two sects at a border.

choices.text: Feed it, talk to it, sit with it

effects.log: By the second week the cat sleeps on your feet. By the fourth, on your chest. You will tell nobody.

choices.text: Keep to your own side of the house

effects.log: A month of armed truce. When {npc} comes home, the cat runs to {him} and you are both pretending you are fine.

events.text: {npc} comes home a day early and finds you asleep in the sun, with the grey cat asleep on your chest and your hand on its back. {He} stands in the doorway a long time before {he} says anything.

choices.text: Deny everything

mem.note: was caught being kind to the cat

effects.log: 'The cat lay on me,' you say. 'I was trapped.' {npc} tells this story at every festival for the rest of your lives.

choices.text: Admit you love the cat

effects.log: {npc} sits down beside you both. That night the cat sleeps between you, which it has never done before.

events.text: The teapot breaks. It was {npc}'s grandmother's, and it was you who knocked it off the table, and you who said, before thinking, that it was an ugly teapot anyway. The room has gone very cold.

choices.text: Apologise at once, for both things

mem.note: broke the teapot, then said sorry

effects.log: {npc} accepts the first apology and not the second. 'It was an ugly teapot,' {he} says. 'It was mine.'

choices.text: Say nothing, and gather the pieces

effects.log: You pick up every piece, even the small ones under the cupboard, and wrap them in cloth. {npc} watches, saying nothing.

choices.text: Buy a finer teapot the next day (20 taels)

mem.note: thought a teapot could be bought

effects.log: The new teapot is very fine. {npc} thanks you and puts it on a high shelf, and does not use it. (-20 taels)

events.text: The quarrel has not ended. It has only gone quiet. Then you hear of a mender in the next town who joins broken pottery with lacquer and gold, so the cracks shine instead of hiding.

choices.text: Take the pieces to the mender (30 taels)

effects.log: The mender works for a month. The teapot comes back whole, with veins of gold across it like rivers on a map. (-30 taels)

choices.text: Ask {npc} about the grandmother

effects.log: {npc} talks for an hour about a fierce old woman who made tea for bandits once and talked them out of a raid. You listen to all of it.

choices.text: Let it go quiet and wait

effects.log: The quiet lasts a month and then wears off, like frost. Nobody won. The teapot is still in pieces in a cloth.

events.text: The teapot with the golden cracks stands on the table, or the story of the grandmother sits between you, whichever it was. {npc} pours tea and says, looking at the cup, 'I said things too. That day.'

choices.text: Say you remember nothing but the teapot

effects.log: {npc} smiles into the cup. The quarrel is over. Somehow it has left the house a little stronger, like the pot.

choices.text: Say what you were sorry for, all of it

mem.note: said sorry for all of it

effects.log: You both say it. It takes a long time and a second pot. At the end the tea is cold and you are both warm.

events.text: You were meant to be gone three months, to train in the mountains. It has been a year and a half. You come home with a new technique and an old travel cloak, and find the gate barred, and {npc} on the other side of it.

choices.text: Knock, and keep knocking

effects.log: You knock till dusk. The gate opens a crack. {npc} looks at you, and says the guest room is made up, and closes it again.

choices.text: Sit at the gate and wait, as long as it takes

effects.log: Two nights at the gate in the cold. On the third morning there is a bowl of porridge beside you, with no word.

choices.text: Climb the wall

ok.log: You land in the courtyard. {npc} is waiting with a broom. You deserved that, and the broom agrees.

fail.log: You fall off the wall into the gutter. Somewhere inside, {npc} laughs once, very hard, and then remembers to be angry.

events.text: You are home, but you are a guest in your own house. {npc} has run everything for a year and a half: the roof, the accounts, the quarrel with the neighbours about the drain. {He} did it well, and alone, and {he} wants you to know it.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to show you everything, and listen

mem.note: listened to what I carried alone

effects.log: It takes three days. You learn about the drain, and the roof, and the night {npc} sat up alone in a storm. You listen to all of it.

choices.text: Take over the work again, at once

mem.note: took my work back without asking

effects.log: {npc} lets you, and watches you do it wrong. The quarrel with the neighbours begins again on your first day.

choices.text: Show {npc} the technique you learned

mem.note: thought a technique made up for it

effects.log: It is a beautiful technique. {npc} watches, and says, 'That is what a year and a half looks like,' and goes inside.

events.text: The first snow. {npc} finds you on the roof at dawn, mending the place over the bedroom that leaked all last winter while you were away. You have been at it for hours. Your hands are blue.

choices.text: Say you should have been here last winter

effects.log: {npc} climbs up the ladder, sits beside you on the cold tiles and holds the next tile while you nail it.

choices.text: Promise never to be gone so long again

mem.note: promised to come home on time

effects.log: 'You will,' {npc} says. 'You are you.' {He} hands you hot tea anyway. 'But write next time.'

events.text: A bad day at the sect, a worse one at home, and at supper you say something to {npc} that you do not mean, and that cuts exactly where you knew it would. {npc} puts down {his} chopsticks and leaves the table.

choices.text: Follow at once and apologise

mem.note: said a cruel thing, then came after me

effects.log: {npc} lets you say it, all of it, at the door of the study. Then says, 'I know. I still heard it.' The door closes.

choices.text: Let {npc} be alone tonight

effects.log: You sit alone with the cold supper. The house is very quiet. You hear the words again and again, in your own voice.

choices.text: Insist you were right

mem.note: said a cruel thing and stood by it

effects.log: You say it again, louder. You win the argument. You lose something else, and you can feel it go.

events.text: A week of politeness. {npc} is very correct with you, like a host with a guest. The servants walk on tiptoe. You find yourself at the market, looking at nothing, trying to think of what would actually mend it.

choices.text: Write it down, every word, and what you really meant

effects.log: Four pages. You leave them on {npc}'s pillow. The next morning they are gone, and {npc} is at breakfast, red-eyed, and smiles once.

choices.text: Say sorry in front of the whole household

mem.note: said sorry in front of everyone

effects.log: The servants do not know where to look. {npc} does: straight at you. 'Fine,' {he} says. 'Fine. Sit down.'

choices.text: Make the thing you said untrue

effects.log: You said {npc} never finishes anything. You spend a month helping {him} finish the thing {he} started years ago. It is done.

events.text: Years later, in a quarrel about nothing, you feel the same cruel words rising in your throat, the old ones, ready. {npc} sees it in your face. {He} waits, to see what you will do.

choices.text: Swallow them, and laugh at yourself

effects.log: You laugh. {npc} laughs too, from relief. The quarrel about nothing ends in nothing, which is how it should.

choices.text: Say: I almost said it again

mem.note: told me the truth about the words

effects.log: 'I know,' {npc} says. 'I saw.' And takes your hand, because you did not.

events.text: {npc} keeps the household ledger, and the ledger says you have spent ninety taels this year on 'swords, various'. You have one sword. You are not sure yourself where the other eighty-five taels went.

choices.text: Confess: a sword-polishing master, very expensive

effects.log: {npc} closes the ledger slowly. 'Polish,' {he} says. 'Eighty-five taels of polish.' You nod. You will hear of it for a decade.

choices.text: Demand to see what {npc} spent too

ok.log: Sixty taels on 'tea, rare'. You both sit in silence with the ledger between you, and then you both start laughing.

fail.log: {npc}'s accounts are perfect, to the copper. Yours are a crime scene. You sleep in the study.

choices.text: Hand over your purse for a year

effects.log: {npc} takes it, counts it, and gives you an allowance like a child. The house runs better at once. (-30 taels)

events.text: A household budget, drawn up by {npc} and nailed to the kitchen door. It has columns. It has a column for you, called 'swords, various', with a limit of five taels a month. The servants have read it. The neighbours have read it.

choices.text: Keep to it, exactly, for a whole year

effects.log: A year of five taels a month. At the end of it there is silver in the chest and {npc} buys you a very fine sword. (+20 taels)

choices.text: Add a column for {npc}: tea, rare

effects.log: {npc} sees it, takes the brush, and raises both limits. 'For peace,' {he} says. The servants cheer.

choices.text: Earn the difference on the side

effects.log: Guard work, three nights a month. Your column is never short again. {npc} is suspicious and proud. (+15 taels)

events.text: At the year's end feast, {npc} reads the ledger aloud as a toast, as is the custom of the house now. The last line is in {his} hand, new: 'Spent on the one I married: everything. Worth: all of it.'

choices.text: Raise your cup and say nothing

effects.log: Nobody in the hall says anything either. Then the cook starts crying, and everybody laughs, and the feast goes on.

choices.text: Take the brush and add a line of your own

effects.log: Your line is shorter and worse spelled. {npc} keeps that page when the ledger is full, folded in a drawer.

events.text: It began with the window: open or shut. It has become a contest. Neither you nor {npc} has spoken a word in a day, and neither will be the first. You communicate entirely through the cook, who is very tired.

choices.text: Hold out. You can outlast anyone

effects.log: The cook now carries messages on paper. 'Tell the master of the house the soup is cold.' 'Tell the other one it was cold on purpose.'

choices.text: Write notes instead of speaking

effects.log: Notes are not speaking. {npc} agrees, in a note. By evening there are forty notes and one very confused cat.

choices.text: Speak first, and lose

effects.log: 'Leave the window open,' you say. {npc} smiles like a general after a battle. You lose the war and win dinner.

events.text: The third day. A guest of rank is coming tonight, and a household where nobody speaks will be very strange at dinner. {npc} is watching you over the teacups. Somebody will have to crack.

choices.text: Let the guest arrive and see what happens

ok.log: You both speak only to the guest, beautifully, all evening. The guest leaves saying it was the best dinner of the year.

fail.log: The guest asks if someone has died. The cook bursts into tears. You and {npc} both speak at once, to apologise.

choices.text: Start to laugh, out loud, which is not speaking

effects.log: {npc} laughs too. Neither of you has technically spoken. You declare it a draw, in writing.

choices.text: Shut the window, slowly, while looking at {npc}

effects.log: {npc} opens it again. You shut it. The guest arrives to find you both at the window, shouting. Silence over.

events.text: It has become a story the whole street knows: the Three Days. Every year on that date, the two of you keep one hour of silence together, at the window, to remember how stupid you both were. This year {npc} breaks it first.

choices.text: Claim the victory, twenty years late

effects.log: 'It does not count,' {npc} says. 'It is a different war.' You argue happily about the rules until supper.

choices.text: Ask what {he} wanted to say

mem.note: asked what I wanted to say

effects.log: 'Only that I would still choose you,' {npc} says. 'Window and all.' You leave it open that night.

events.text: A letter comes for you from someone you loved long before {npc}: a sweetheart from your youth, now widowed, in a far province. It is a kind letter, about old times. {npc} hands it to you, already opened, with a face like a frozen pond.

choices.text: Read it aloud, at the table

effects.log: There is nothing in it but old times and a cough. {npc} listens, and thaws a little, and asks who the cousin with the goat was.

choices.text: Burn it unread

effects.log: You burn it. {npc} watches it burn and says, 'Now I will never know what it said.' This was not the result you wanted.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to write the reply with you

mem.note: let me write the reply with you

effects.log: {npc} writes most of it. It is a very kind reply, and signs both your names, very large.

events.text: The old sweetheart from the letter is passing through on a pilgrimage and asks to call on you. {npc} has already started cleaning the house as if for an emperor, and refuses to say why.

choices.text: Invite the old sweetheart, and stay by {npc} all evening

effects.log: The old sweetheart is grey, funny and kind, and spends the evening talking to {npc}, not you. They part as friends. You are slightly offended.

choices.text: Meet the old sweetheart at the teahouse, alone

effects.log: A pleasant hour at the teahouse. You come home and find the house cleaned to the bone, and {npc} cold for a week.

choices.text: Send apologies, and keep the past in the past

mem.note: kept the past in the past

effects.log: The old sweetheart sends back a pear and a blessing for your house. {npc} eats the pear, all of it, thoughtfully.

events.text: {npc} has been thinking. 'Tell me about before me,' {he} says. 'All of it. I would rather know you than guess at you.'

choices.text: Tell all of it, honestly

effects.log: It takes a long evening. Some of it is foolish and some of it is sad. {npc} listens like a judge, then like a friend.

choices.text: Tell it, and then ask for {his} too

effects.log: {npc}'s past has a fisherman in it, and a duel, and a bad poem. By midnight you are both laughing at your younger selves.

events.text: The sect calls you away again on the night of the family supper you promised {npc} you would not miss. A messenger waits at the gate. {npc} is standing at the kitchen door with a ladle and an expression.

choices.text: Go with the messenger

mem.note: left the supper for the sect

effects.log: The sect's business takes all night and turns out to be nothing much. You come home to a cold supper and a colder spouse.

choices.text: Send the messenger back with your excuses

effects.log: The elders are displeased. The supper is wonderful. {npc} does not say anything, but gives you the best piece of fish.

choices.text: Bring the messenger in to eat first

effects.log: The messenger eats three bowls and forgets the message for an hour. You leave late, well fed, with {npc}'s blessing, sort of.

events.text: {npc} has written a list. It is the list of every supper, festival and birthday you missed for the sect in the last ten years. It is very long. {He} does not shout. {He} only hands it to you and waits.

choices.text: Go to the elders and ask for fewer night calls

mem.note: asked the elders for our evenings

effects.log: The elders grumble, then agree: one night a week is the house's. The sect survives. So does the supper.

choices.text: Promise to do better, and mean it

effects.log: {npc} folds the list and puts it away, not in the fire. 'We will see,' {he} says. Fair.

choices.text: Say the sect feeds this house

effects.log: It is true. It is also the wrong thing to say. {npc} keeps the list, and adds that evening to it.

events.text: A messenger at the gate again, on supper night. This time, before you can move, {npc} goes out to the gate, speaks to the messenger, and comes back. 'It can wait till morning,' {he} says. 'I asked. Sit.'

choices.text: Sit

effects.log: You sit. The supper is long and loud and happy. In the morning the sect's business is still there, and smaller.

choices.text: Laugh, and ask what {he} told the messenger

mem.note: laughed with me at the gate

effects.log: 'That you were ill with a terrible hunger,' {npc} says. The messenger ate with the servants. Everyone won.

events.text: Your sword is not on its rack. It is not in the well, the granary or the carp pond, all of which you check. At breakfast {npc} and the newest member of the household, who have not agreed about anything since the day they met, pass each other the pickles with a strange new courtesy.
events.arc: The Treaty of the Missing Sword

choices.text: Ask the table, sweetly, where your sword is

effects.log: "What sword?" says {npc}. The newest member of the household nods along. They have rehearsed this. You are almost proud.

choices.text: Search their rooms while they eat

ok.log: The sword is under {npc}'s bedding, wrapped in a quilt like a baby, with a note pinned to it: ASK US WHY.

fail.log: You are caught with your head in a clothes chest. Breakfast becomes a hearing.

choices.text: Buy a new sword at the market (30 taels)

effects.log: By noon the new sword has vanished as well. The pickles at dinner are passed with great politeness.

events.text: {npc} lays a sheet of paper before you, written in two hands. It is a treaty. Article one: the sword is returned. Article two: it may leave the house only with a note signed by two spouses. Article three, underlined twice: no more duels with anyone whose name ends in Demon.
events.arc: The Treaty of the Missing Sword

choices.text: Sign it

effects.log: {npc} blows on your signature like a magistrate. The sword comes back polished, oiled and wearing a tassel.

choices.text: Negotiate article three

ok.log: Article three is amended to names ending in Demon, Devil or Butcher. You call it a victory. So do they.

fail.log: You argue for an hour. Article three now has an article four, about arguing.

choices.text: Refuse, and train with a broom

effects.log: You train with a broom in the yard every morning, with dignity. The whole house watches from the windows, eating melon seeds.

events.text: A wandering swordsman called Iron Gourd Pak arrives at your gate with a challenge, a crowd and no idea about the treaty. You need two signatures by noon. {npc} is at the market. The newest member of the household is asleep. Iron Gourd Pak is doing stretches.
events.arc: The Treaty of the Missing Sword

choices.text: Run to the market for a signature

ok.log: You come back with both signatures and one cabbage, beat Iron Gourd Pak in six moves, and are home for lunch.

fail.log: By the time you have both names, Iron Gourd Pak has grown bored and gone. A child tells the street you hid.

choices.text: Decline the duel, citing the treaty

effects.log: "I am under treaty," you tell the crowd. Iron Gourd Pak, who is also married, nods with deep understanding and goes home.

choices.text: Fight with the broom

effects.log: You beat Iron Gourd Pak with a broom. The treaty never said anything about brooms. {npc} adds an article that night.

events.text: The household comes to your next duel without being asked: {npc}, the others, two servants, a basket of dumplings and a straw mat. They sit at the edge of the duelling ground and cheer every parry. Your opponent's own household, it turns out, has been doing the same thing from the far side for years.
events.arc: The Treaty of the Missing Sword

choices.text: Win it for them

ok.log: You win cleanly. The cheering from the mat is louder than the cheering from the crowd.

fail.log: You lose. The dumplings are excellent anyway, and both households share them on one mat.

choices.text: Invite the other household onto your mat

effects.log: Two households, one mat, one duel that nobody is watching any more. The dumplings run out first.

choices.text: Ask them, gently, to go home

effects.log: They go home. Halfway through the duel you lose your concentration, looking for the mat.

events.text: The old pine chair at {npc}'s place has carried {him} through every meal since the house was one room. Tonight a leg gives way in the middle of the soup. Nobody laughs. Everybody very carefully does not laugh. {npc} finishes the soup standing.

choices.text: Give {npc} your own chair

effects.log: You sit on an upturned rice basket. {npc} sits in your chair and looks, for one meal, enormously amused.

choices.text: Have it mended by morning (8 taels)

effects.log: The carpenter works by lamplight. The new leg is a shade darker than the others, like a scar that is proud of itself.

choices.text: Make a joke about the soup

effects.log: The joke is good. It is not the night for it. {npc} thanks you for it very politely.

events.text: The newest member of the household, who carves wood, has made {npc} a new chair: camphor wood, carved cranes, a cushion of red silk. It is presented at breakfast before the whole house. {npc} looks at it, then at the old chair, then at you.

choices.text: Praise the new chair

effects.log: The newcomer glows. {npc} sits in the crane chair, very upright, as if it might bite.

choices.text: Say {npc} should choose

effects.log: {npc} thanks the newcomer warmly, then asks if the cranes could be carved onto the old chair instead. They can.

choices.text: Sit in the new chair yourself

effects.log: It is the best chair you have ever sat in. Everyone laughs. The problem is now yours, which is how {npc} likes problems.

events.text: Years later, out of nowhere, {npc} asks who will sit in the old chair after {he} is gone. The house is listening from three doorways. It is not a gloomy question, {he} says. It is a practical one.

choices.text: Say nobody, ever

mem.note: said nobody would take my chair

effects.log: "Sentimental," says {npc}, and smiles into {his} tea for the rest of the evening.

choices.text: Say whoever keeps the house best

effects.log: Three doorways go quiet. Every member of the household starts keeping the house better at once. {npc} is very pleased with the question.

choices.text: Say you will, to keep it warm

effects.log: "You would break it in a week," says {npc}. But {he} has the darker leg strengthened the very next day.

events.text: The newest member of the household has brought a cook from a southern province, and three sacks of red peppers. Your own cook, who has fed the house for twenty years, has stopped speaking. {npc}, who loves plain rice above all things, ate one southern dumpling at dinner and has not yet recovered.

choices.text: Let both cooks cook

effects.log: Two kitchens, two smells, one courtyard of very confused cats. The meals are magnificent and the cooks are at war.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to rule the kitchens

effects.log: {npc} divides the days: odd days plain, even days fiery. The calendar is pinned to the kitchen door with a cleaver.

choices.text: Eat at the noodle stalls for a month

effects.log: The noodle seller hears the whole story over a month of lunches and takes a side.

events.text: The war of the kitchens has reached the ancestral feast. Each cook has prepared the whole menu, in secret, and both menus arrive at once: forty dishes on a table built for twenty. {npc} stands at the head of it holding a bowl of plain rice like a shield.

choices.text: Eat from both, loudly

effects.log: You eat everything and praise everything. You lie down for a day afterwards, and both cooks visit you with soup.

choices.text: Hold a contest, and judge it

ok.log: You call it a draw and order the two cooks to make one dish together. The kitchen goes very quiet.

fail.log: You choose a winner. The loser packs a bag. It takes {npc} three days to unpack it.

choices.text: Send the second menu out to the street

effects.log: Twenty dishes go out of the gate to the beggars of the district, who have strong opinions about the peppers.

events.text: One morning the two cooks come to you together, floured to the elbows. Between them they have made a dish: the old kitchen's plain rice and the south's red peppers, folded into one dumpling. They want you to name it. {npc} has already eaten four.

choices.text: Name it after {npc}

effects.log: Within a year it is sold at the district market under {npc}'s name. {npc} is mortified, and buys a dozen every market day.

choices.text: Name it after the house

effects.log: House Dumplings, says the sign. Pilgrims come asking for them. The two cooks are rude to the pilgrims together.

choices.text: Sell the recipe to a merchant

effects.log: The merchant pays well. The cooks are flattered and offended at once, and invent a better dumpling out of spite.

events.text: The newest member of the household is better than you at the abacus, at the zither, at the rites and, as of this morning in the yard, at the spear. {npc} watched the spear lesson from the veranda with a cup of tea and an expression of quiet, enormous joy.

choices.text: Ask the newcomer for lessons

effects.log: You are a poor student and the newcomer a patient teacher. {npc} brings out a second cup and a stool to watch.

choices.text: Demand a rematch

ok.log: You win the rematch, narrowly. Nobody, least of all you, is sure the newcomer did not let you.

fail.log: You lose faster than the first time. The whole house is very kind about it, which is worse.

choices.text: Ask {npc} what is so funny

effects.log: "Nothing," says {npc}. "For twenty years you were the best at everything in this house. I am enjoying the weather."

events.text: You find the newcomer at night in the woodshed, practising the spear by lamplight with raw hands, and crying a little. "Everyone here has a place," they say. "I only have the things I am good at." Behind you, {npc} has come out with a lantern too.

choices.text: Let {npc} speak to them

effects.log: {npc} sits on the chopping block and tells the newcomer about the leaking roof and the lean first years. They come in together, late.

choices.text: Admit you have been jealous

effects.log: The newcomer stares, then laughs through the tears. "Of me?" You both look at {npc}, who is plainly the real winner here.

choices.text: Bandage their hands and send them to bed

effects.log: You bandage the hands badly. The newcomer keeps the bandages on for two days longer than needed.

events.text: The newcomer now teaches the spear to half the district's children in your yard, every morning, for nothing. {npc} keeps the register of names. You have been given the job of fetching water for the students, and you are less unhappy about it than you expected.

choices.text: Fetch the water with dignity

effects.log: Two buckets, forty trips. The children call you Water Elder. Within a month so does the whole district.

choices.text: Ask to teach one morning a week

ok.log: Your morning becomes the popular one, because you tell stories between the forms.

fail.log: Your morning is the one the children skip. The newcomer kindly pretends not to notice.

choices.text: Charge the families a small fee

effects.log: Fewer children come. The newcomer is quietly disappointed, and {npc} returns the fees in your name.

events.text: You come home from a year of closed-door training to find the gate repainted, the accounts in surplus, the gutter mended and a new rule painted over the hall door: NO SWORDS AT DINNER. {npc} greets you at the gate with a warm bow and the faint air of a ruler receiving a visiting dignitary.
events.arc: The House That Ran Better Without You

choices.text: Thank everyone for keeping the house

effects.log: Everyone is touched. Then they go back to running the house around you, like water around a stone.

choices.text: Ask to see the accounts

effects.log: The accounts are perfect. Your old method has been retired, with a little note in the margin: "too creative".

choices.text: Take your old seat at the head of the hall

effects.log: You sit in your old seat. The meetings quietly move to the kitchen. You only find out a month later.

events.text: There is a meeting of the household every fifth day. You are not invited. You learn this from a servant who assumed you knew. Through the screen you hear {npc} say: "Item three. What to do about the head of the house."
events.arc: The House That Ran Better Without You

choices.text: Listen at the screen

ok.log: Item three is your birthday. Item four is whether you are lonely. You go away very quietly, and very moved.

fail.log: You knock over a vase. The whole meeting comes out to look at you. Item three is postponed.

choices.text: Knock and walk in

effects.log: "Item three has arrived," says {npc}. "Sit down." You are given a stool and no vote.

choices.text: Hold a rival meeting of one

effects.log: You hold a meeting with yourself in the study, with minutes. The minutes are leaked. The house laughs for a week.

events.text: The household presents you with a carved wooden tablet: Honorary Member of the Household Council. It comes with a stool, a vote on all matters of the carp pond, and the duty of feeding the carp. {npc} reads out the terms in a perfectly straight voice.
events.arc: The House That Ran Better Without You

choices.text: Accept, with a speech

effects.log: Your speech is long. They let you finish. The carp have never been so well fed.

choices.text: Demand a vote on dinner too

ok.log: Granted, on fish days only. You count it a famous triumph.

fail.log: Refused, unanimously, including by the cook, who is not on the council.

choices.text: Feed the carp and say nothing

effects.log: The carp pond is very peaceful. Within a year it is where the household comes to find you, and they do.

events.text: Someone has filled {npc}'s writing brushes with ink from the wrong end, tied bells to every cat in the house and painted a moustache on the ancestor in the hall portrait. Each courtyard blames the children of the other courtyards. The children of every courtyard look like saints.
events.arc: The Gang of the Inner Courtyards

choices.text: Question the children one by one

ok.log: Every child gives the same alibi, word for word. It is the first thing all your children have ever done together.

fail.log: The questioning turns into a quarrel among the grown-ups. The children watch it with deep satisfaction.

choices.text: Laugh at the moustache

effects.log: You laugh. {npc} tries very hard not to, and fails. The others start laughing too, guiltily.

choices.text: Punish all the children equally

effects.log: Every child copies the household rules ten times, in one room, together, conspiring.

events.text: The pranks have grown ambitious. Last night the carp pond was dyed red. This morning every pair of shoes in the house was found on the roof, in neat rows. {npc} has stopped blaming anyone's child in particular. "They have formed a sect," {he} says. "We are the enemy sect."
events.arc: The Gang of the Inner Courtyards

choices.text: Plan a counter-prank with the grown-ups

ok.log: The grown-ups of the house plot together for the first time in years. It is the best evening the house has had.

fail.log: A child uncovers your counter-prank in an hour. The children are very kind about it.

choices.text: Offer the children a truce, with sweets

effects.log: The children accept the sweets and refuse the truce. They are scrupulously fair about it.

choices.text: Leave it to {npc}

effects.log: {npc} takes away the ladder to the roof. That is all. The pranks stop for a month, out of respect.

events.text: The children of the house, older now, finally confess. It was never about mischief, they say. The grown-ups used to eat in separate courtyards. Since the first moustache, everyone has eaten in one hall, to keep an eye on the children.
events.arc: The Gang of the Inner Courtyards

choices.text: Tell them it worked

effects.log: It worked. You all still eat in one hall. Your children are insufferably proud of themselves, and are allowed to be.

choices.text: Pretend to be angry for one more minute

effects.log: One minute of thunder. Then {npc} bursts out laughing and the thunder is over for good.

choices.text: Keep the moustache on the ancestor

effects.log: The ancestor keeps the moustache. Visitors are told it was always there. In time, it was.

events.text: The newest member of the household has been lighting incense at night, alone, before a small wooden tablet with an unfamiliar name: the elders of their own line, long gone, who have nobody else left to remember them. {npc} found out first and has told no one, which is not like {him}.

choices.text: Ask {npc} what should be done

effects.log: "A hall has room for more than one line of names," {npc} says at last. "But ask the clan elders first, or they will never forgive us."

choices.text: Offer the newcomer a place in the hall

effects.log: The newcomer weeps with gratitude. {npc} is hurt that you did not ask {him} first, and says so, once.

choices.text: Leave it be. It is private

effects.log: You say nothing. The incense keeps burning at night. It is not your grief to manage.

events.text: Three elders of the clan arrive in their best robes to object, in turns, to a strange tablet in the ancestral hall. {npc} has prepared tea, cushions and a scroll of precedents going back four hundred years.

choices.text: Let {npc} argue the case

effects.log: {npc} cites eleven precedents. The elders cite two. By the third pot of tea they are arguing about another family entirely.

choices.text: Argue it yourself

ok.log: You speak plainly about remembering the dead. The eldest elder nods slowly and asks for more tea.

fail.log: You lose your temper at the second precedent. {npc} has to rescue you with the third.

choices.text: Soften the elders with ginseng (20 taels)

effects.log: The elders accept the ginseng, and the tablet. {npc} calls it unnecessary, and writes down which elder took the most.

events.text: At the spring rites the new tablet stands at the end of the row, a little smaller than the rest. The newest member of the household kneels beside {npc}, who shows them where to put their hands. Afterwards the whole house eats together under the plum trees.

choices.text: Kneel with them

effects.log: You kneel too. The smoke of two lines of names goes up together into one sky.

choices.text: Have the new tablet carved to match (10 taels)

effects.log: The new tablet is carved to match the others. The newcomer runs their fingers over the name for a long time.

choices.text: Write the names into the clan book

effects.log: You write the names in your own hand. Now they cannot be forgotten without forgetting your whole house.

events.text: {npc} has a fever and refuses, absolutely, to be ill. {He} has been found keeping the accounts in bed, then in the kitchen, then in the granary. The physician wants {him} lying down for a month. The household wants to know who will run things in the meantime.

choices.text: Run the house yourself

effects.log: You run the house for three days. On the fourth, the cook, the steward and two spouses arrive with lists. You were not aware of lists.

choices.text: Hand the keys to the newest member

effects.log: The newcomer, who has quarrelled with {npc} for a year, takes the keys with shaking hands.

choices.text: Keep {npc} in bed, kindly

effects.log: You sit on the end of the bed with a book and read aloud until {npc} gives up. It takes four days.

events.text: Every morning a bowl of soup appears outside {npc}'s door, with no note. It is the best soup in the house, and the cook did not make it. On the ninth morning you rise early and catch the newest member of the household setting it down, then running.

choices.text: Tell {npc} who brings the soup

effects.log: {npc} is silent a long while. "Of all of them," {he} says. {He} eats the soup slowly, and asks for the recipe.

choices.text: Keep the secret

effects.log: You keep it. On the twentieth morning {npc} is waiting at the door with a second bowl, and the two of them eat in the corridor.

choices.text: Bring {npc} soup of your own as well

effects.log: Yours is much worse. {npc} eats both bowls, out of politeness and then out of hunger.

events.text: {npc} is well. The first thing {he} does is take back the keys. The second, to everyone's astonishment, is to invite the newest member of the household to keep the accounts with {him}: two brushes, one desk.

choices.text: Order a second desk

effects.log: They refuse the second desk. They want to argue over one. Every argument, the house notices, now ends in laughter.

choices.text: Ask {npc} how it happened

effects.log: {npc} shrugs. "Nobody brings soup for nine days to someone they hate. I had to admit it."

choices.text: Take a long holiday while it lasts

effects.log: You spend a month fishing. Nobody misses you at all, which is the best compliment a house can pay.

events.text: An old acquaintance of yours arrives at the gate with a letter of proposal and a box of pears: they would like to join your household. {npc} reads the letter, gathers the others, and announces that the house will hold an entrance examination, as a sect does. You are not on the board.

choices.text: Agree to the examination

effects.log: {npc} writes out three trials on red paper. The applicant reads them and asks for more pears.

choices.text: Send the applicant home kindly

effects.log: The applicant goes home with the pears. {npc} pretends to be disappointed that the examination is off.

choices.text: Insist that you choose, not the house

mem.note: would not let the house choose

effects.log: "Of course," says {npc}, and holds the examination anyway, in the kitchen, with you watching from the door.

events.text: The examination. Trial one: carry a full teapot across the courtyard while three spouses ask hard questions. Trial two: name every servant. Trial three, which {npc} added this morning: tell an honest story about the head of the house. Everybody has come to watch.

choices.text: Watch from the gallery

effects.log: The applicant passes trial one, fails trial two, and tells a story about you and a mule that makes {npc} laugh until {he} cries.

choices.text: Cheer for the applicant

effects.log: Your cheering is noted on the board's paper. The applicant loses points for it.

choices.text: Sit the examination yourself

ok.log: You pass all three trials, barely. The board rules that you may stay.

fail.log: You fail trial two. You did not know the name of the gatekeeper's nephew. The house is shocked.

events.text: The board has met. {npc} hands you the verdict, sealed in red. The applicant is waiting at the gate with an empty pear box. Whatever the paper says, {npc} tells you, the house will abide by it. And so, {he} adds, will you.

choices.text: Open it before everyone

effects.log: Not admitted, but welcome at every feast. The applicant laughs with relief and becomes the house's favourite guest.

choices.text: Ask {npc} privately what it says

effects.log: "That this house is full of people who love you," says {npc}, "and that one more would need a bigger table."

choices.text: Burn it unread and decide yourself
